danish.title: Fjerde bog (1806) — Kapitel 5
paragraphs: »Nå, begynd!« sagde Dolokhov.

»Godt,« sagde Pierre, stadig med det samme smil. En fornemmelse af rædsel lå i luften. Det stod klart, at den sag, der så let var begyndt, ikke længere kunne afværges, men gik sin gang uafhængigt af menneskelig vilje.
Denisov gik først til barrieren og forkyndte: »Da modstandewne har afslået fowsoning, væw så venlig at begynde. Tag Dewes pistolow, og ved owdet twe begyndes fwemwykning.«
»E-en! T-o! Twe!« råbte han vredt og trådte til side.

Duellantterne gik fremad langs de optrampede spor, nærmere og nærmere hinanden, og begyndte at skimte hinanden gennem disen. De havde ret til at skyde, når som helst de ville, mens de nærmede sig barrieren. Dolokhov gik langsomt uden at løfte sin pistol og så opmærksomt med sine klare, funklende blå øjne ind i sin modstanders ansigt. Hans mund bar sit sædvanlige skær af et smil.

»Så jeg kan skyde, når jeg vil!« sagde Pierre, og ved ordet »tre« gik han hurtigt fremad, trådte ved siden af det optrampede spor og ud i den dybe sne. Han holdt pistolen i sin højre hånd med strakt arm, tilsyneladende bange for at skyde sig selv med den. Venstre hånd holdt han omhyggeligt tilbage, fordi han gerne ville støtte højre hånd med den og vidste, at det måtte han ikke. Da han havde tilbagelagt seks skridt og var kommet ud i sneen, kiggede Pierre ned på sine fødder, kastede derefter et hurtigt blik mod Dolokhov, bøjede fingeren, som han var blevet vist, og affyrede. Slet ikke forberedt på det høje brag rystede Pierre ved lyden og stod så stille med et smil over sine egne fornemmelser. Røgen, der var gjort tættere af disen, hindrede ham et øjeblik i at se noget, men der lød intet andet skud, som han havde ventet. Han hørte kun Dolokhov's hastende skridt, og gennem røgen dukkede hans skikkelse op. Han pressede den ene hånd mod sin venstre side, mens den anden klamrede sig om den sænkede pistol. Hans ansigt var blegt. Rostov løb hen til ham og sagde noget.

»Nej-j-j!« mumlede Dolokhov mellem sammenbidt tænder, »nej, det er ikke forbi.« Og efter at have vaklet et par snublende skridt lige hen til sablen sank han ned i sneen ved siden af den. Hans venstre hånd var blodig; han tørrede den på sin frakke og støttede sig med den. Hans sammenbidt ansigt var blegt og dirrede.
»Vær så ...« begyndte Dolokhov, men kunne ikke straks udtale ordet.
»Vær så venlig,« sagde han med en anstrengelse.
Pierre, der næppe kunne holde sine hulk tilbage, begyndte at løbe mod Dolokhov og var ved at krydse pladsen mellem barriererne, da Dolokhov råbte:

»Til Deres barriere!« og Pierre, der forstod, hvad det betød, standsede ved sin sabel. Kun ti skridt skilte dem. Dolokhov sænkede hovedet mod sneen, bed grådigt i den, løftede atter hovedet, rettede sig op, trak benene ind og satte sig, idet han søgte et fast tyngdepunkt. Han sugede og slugte den kolde sne, hans læber skælvede, men hans øjne, stadig smilende, glinsede af anstrengelse og ophidselse, mens han samlede sin sidste kraft. Han løftede pistolen og sigtede.
»Gå til siden! Dæk Dem med Deres pistol!« råbte Nesvitskij.
»Dæk Dem!« råbte selv Denisov til sin modstander.

Pierre, med et mildt smil af medlidenhed og anger og med arme og ben hjælpeløst spredt ud, stod med sit brede bryst vendt direkte mod Dolokhov og så sorgfuldt på ham. Denisov, Rostov og Nesvitskij lukkede øjnene. I samme øjeblik hørte de et skud og Dolokhov's vrede råb.
»Forbandet!« råbte Dolokhov og lå hjælpeløst med ansigtet ned i sneen.
Pierre greb sig til tindingerne, vendte om og gik ind i skoven, mens han trampede gennem den dybe sne og mumlede usammenhængende ord:
»Tåbelighed ... tåbelighed! Død ... løgn ...« gentog han og fordrejede ansigtet.
Nesvitskij standsede ham og kørte ham hjem.
Rostov og Denisov kørte bort med den sårede Dolokhov.

Denne lå tavs i slæden med lukkede øjne og svarede ikke et ord til de spørgsmål, der blev rettet til ham. Men da de kørte ind i Moskva, kom han pludselig til sig selv, løftede med besvær hovedet, tog Rostov, der sad ved hans side, i hånden. Rostov blev slået af det fuldstændig forandrede og uventet henrykte, ømme udtryk i Dolokhov's ansigt.
»Nå? Hvordan har du det?« spurgte han.

»Skidt! Men det er ikke det, min ven —« sagde Dolokhov med en stakåndet stemme. »Hvor er vi? I Moskva, det ved jeg. Mig gør det ikke noget, men hende har jeg dræbt, dræbt ... Hun overlever det ikke! Hun overlever det ikke ...«
»Hvem?« spurgte Rostov.
»Min mor! Min mor, min engel, min elskede englemor,« og Dolokhov trykkede Rostovs hånd og brast i gråd.

Da han var blevet lidt roligere, forklarede han Rostov, at han boede hos sin mor, som, hvis hun så ham døende, ikke ville overleve det. Han bad indtrængende Rostov om at ride i forvejen og forberede hende.

Rostov red forud for at gøre som han var blevet bedt om, og til sin store overraskelse erfarede han, at Dolokhov — slagsbroderen, bøffen Dolokhov — boede i Moskva med sin gamle mor og en pukkelrygget søster og var den mest hengivne søn og bror.

english.title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 5
paragraphs: "Well, begin!" said Dolokhov.

"All right," said Pierre, still wearing the same smile. A feeling of dread hung in the air. It was clear that this affair, so casually begun, could no longer be stopped — it was taking its own course, beyond anyone's control.
Denisov went first to the barrier and announced: "As the adversaries have refused a reconciliation, please proceed. Take your pistols, and at the word three, begin to advance."
"One! Two! Three!" he shouted angrily, and stepped aside.

The two men advanced along the trampled paths, drawing closer and closer, beginning to make each other out through the mist. They were free to fire whenever they chose as they approached the barrier. Dolokhov walked slowly without raising his pistol, his bright, sparkling blue eyes fixed intently on his opponent's face. His mouth wore its usual hint of a smile.

"So I can fire whenever I want!" said Pierre, and at the word "three" he walked quickly forward, missing the trampled path and stepping into deep snow. He held the pistol in his outstretched right hand, apparently afraid of shooting himself with it. He kept his left hand carefully behind him, because he wanted to steady his right hand with it but knew he wasn't supposed to. After advancing six paces and straying off the path into the snow, Pierre glanced down at his feet, then quickly looked up at Dolokhov and, bending his finger as he'd been shown, fired. Not at all expecting such a loud report, Pierre flinched at the sound and then, smiling at his own reaction, stood still. The smoke, made denser by the mist, blocked his view for a moment, but there was no second shot as he had expected. He only heard Dolokhov's hurried steps, and then his figure emerged through the smoke. He was pressing one hand to his left side while the other clutched his drooping pistol. His face was pale. Rostov ran toward him and said something.

"N-no!" Dolokhov muttered through clenched teeth. "No, it's not over." And after stumbling a few staggering steps right up to the saber marker, he collapsed onto the snow beside it. His left hand was bloody; he wiped it on his coat and propped himself up with it. His frowning face was deathly pale and trembling.
"Plea—" Dolokhov began, but couldn't get the word out at first.
"Please," he managed with effort.
Pierre, barely holding back his sobs, started running toward Dolokhov and was about to cross the space between the barriers when Dolokhov shouted:

"Back to your barrier!" Pierre understood what was meant and stopped by his saber. Only ten paces separated them. Dolokhov lowered his head to the snow and bit at it hungrily, then raised his head again, adjusted his position, drew in his legs, and sat up, searching for a firm center of gravity. He sucked and swallowed the cold snow; his lips quivered, but his eyes, still smiling, glittered with effort and fury as he summoned his remaining strength. He raised his pistol and took aim.
"Sideways! Shield yourself with your pistol!" shouted Nesvitski.
"Take cover!" even Denisov cried out to his opponent.

Pierre, with a gentle smile of pity and remorse, his arms and legs spread helplessly, stood with his broad chest facing Dolokhov directly and looked at him with sorrow. Denisov, Rostov, and Nesvitski squeezed their eyes shut. At that same instant they heard a shot and Dolokhov's furious cry.
"Missed!" Dolokhov shouted, and he lay helplessly face down in the snow.
Pierre clutched his temples and, turning around, walked into the forest, trampling through the deep snow and muttering incoherent words:
"Madness... madness! Death... lies..." he repeated, his face contorted.
Nesvitski stopped him and took him home.
Rostov and Denisov drove away with the wounded Dolokhov.

Dolokhov lay silent in the sleigh with his eyes closed, not answering any of the questions put to him. But as they entered Moscow he suddenly came to and, lifting his head with effort, took hold of Rostov's hand — Rostov was sitting beside him. Rostov was struck by the completely altered, unexpectedly tender and emotional expression on Dolokhov's face.
"Well? How do you feel?" he asked.

"Bad! But that's not it, my friend —" said Dolokhov in a gasping voice. "Where are we? In Moscow, I know. I don't matter, but I've killed her, killed... She won't recover from this! She won't survive...."
"Who?" asked Rostov.
"My mother! My mother, my angel, my beloved angel mother," and Dolokhov squeezed Rostov's hand and burst into tears.
When he had calmed down a little, he explained to Rostov that he was living with his mother, who, if she saw him dying, would not survive it. He begged Rostov to go ahead and prepare her.

Rostov went on ahead to do as asked, and to his great surprise learned that Dolokhov the brawler, Dolokhov the bully, lived in Moscow with an elderly mother and a hunchbacked sister, and was the most devoted of sons and brothers.
